newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - CSCE coffee soars to 15-month highs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - CSCE coffee soars to 15-month highs.

text.p: Arabica coffee futures on the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange (CSCE) in New York surged to fresh life-of-contract highs on Wednesday, as speculators bought heavily on persistent supply concerns.
Coffee for March delivery rose 5.10 cents per lb on the day, to 144.60 cents, after vaulting to a new contract high of 147.80 cents.
Nearby CSCE coffee futures are now at their highest levels since September 1995.
Market sources said projections for a smaller harvest in top-producer Brazil, coupled by news of possible crop damage due to heavy rains in Colombia, have heightened supply worries.
"There is still a lot of uncertainty over Brazil's and Colombia's crop prospects," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt.
Preliminary estimates by the Brazilian Commerce Ministry pegged the country's coming 1997/98 coffee crop between 18 million and 20 million bags, some six million bags lower than a year earlier.
In Colombia, agronomists said heavy downpours over the last three weeks in the country's's principal coffee-growing regions are likely to be affected the main crop harvest which begins in October.
Additionally, sources said Colombian coffee exports have been slow getting to normal following a nine-day dockworkers' strike, which ended last Thursday.
"The bottom line in Colombia is that they are still moving sporadically," one coffee broker said. "There is major backlog and it takes awhile to clean up."

Traders and analysts said low levels of consumer coffee stocks in the U.S. have been at the root of the market's recent surge to their highest levels since September 1995. Since early December, futures have rallied more than 40 percent.

Normally, an increased flow of newly harvested, high quality "arabica" beans from Latin America during the first quarter of the year builds stockpiles, but inventories have hovered at their lowest levels in some 20 years.
"Expectations had been new supplies would be coming in and they haven't," Ganes said. "Whatever has come in has been readily absorbed."
Ganes said aggressive bidding by European roasters has helped absorbed the new crop and U.S. inventories have dwindled.
But some market sources said while underlying fundamentals are bullish, the recent bull run has been fueled by heavy speculative particiation and could be vunerable to a sharp sell-off.
"Some speculators who never traded coffee are trading," one Florida-based coffee broker said.
Open interest in the coffee market is extremely high at 42,957 lots as of January 28, and traders estimated speculative postions accounted for the bulk of it.

"Speculators in the commodity market are only in it for the short-term," one trader said. "Come first notice day February 20 (for the spot March contract) 75 percent of the specs will be out of coffee."
But Ganes said the rally was justifed fundamentally.
"The fact is, the coffee is not there," she said. "Speculators exaggerate the moves, but they don't create the trends."
